\chapter{Reading Older Spanish --- Register, Date, and Form}
\label{ch:literario}
\hlchaptermodality{276}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can tell from small details whether a Spanish text is literary and whether its verse is rhymed.}

Complete ES-C276-practice: say what each detail tells you about a text before you have read it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mas]{mas — a word you will only ever read}

\label{lesson:ES-C276-mas}



\begin{quote}
The last chapter is about Spanish written before you were born, and Spanish written to be read rather than said. This word is both.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item pero — the everyday \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{}.
  \item más que — the comparison, WITH an accent.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mas}, one syllable, unstressed in the sentence — and note it has \textbf{no written accent}, which is the whole point. \emph{Más} with the accent is \textquotedblleft{}more.\textquotedblright{} $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mas} — \textquotedblleft{}but.\textquotedblright{} The same job as \emph{pero}, and almost nobody says it aloud.

It is Latin \textbf{magis}, \textquotedblleft{}more\textquotedblright{} — the same word that gave you \emph{más}. The two split: \emph{más} kept the quantity, \emph{mas} took a contrastive sense and then retreated into books.

The accent is doing real work here, and this is the pair the written accent exists for: \emph{mas} (but) against \emph{más} (more). Two words, one sound, and only the page tells them apart.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word that survives \textbf{only in writing} is a marker of \textbf{literary register}, and a reader needs to recognise it for two reasons.

First, practically: meeting \emph{mas} in a poem and reading it as \emph{más} turns the sentence inside out.

Second, and more usefully: its presence tells you what kind of text you are in before you have understood a word of it. Register is information carried by \textbf{which} words appear, independently of what they say — and a text signals it in the first line.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mas} and \emph{más}, and name the difference on the page
  \item the everyday word it replaces (\emph{pero})
  \item what its presence tells you about a text
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the difference between \emph{mas} and \emph{más}? (But; more — only the accent separates them.) What does meeting \emph{mas} tell you before you have read the sentence? (That the text is literary.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[asonancia]{asonancia — why Spanish poems do not rhyme the way you expect}

\label{lesson:ES-C276-asonancia}



\begin{quote}
The last piece. If Spanish verse has ever sounded to you like it nearly rhymes, this is why.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item mas — the literary register marker.
  \item vuestra merced $\to$ usted — the archaic form, taught long ago.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-so-NAN-cia}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{asonancia} — assonance: rhyme on the \textbf{vowels only}, ignoring the consonants after them.

\emph{Luna} and \emph{cuna} rhyme fully — English would call that a rhyme too. But \emph{luna} and \emph{musa} are also a rhyme in Spanish verse: stressed \emph{u}, final \emph{a}, and the \emph{n} against the \emph{s} simply does not count.

\emph{Asonancia} is Latin \textbf{assonare}, \textquotedblleft{}to sound towards\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ad} plus \emph{sonare}, the root of \textbf{sound}, \textbf{sonorous} and \textbf{unison}.

This is not a loose or lazy rhyme. It is the organising principle of the \textbf{romance}, the ballad form, which runs from medieval oral poetry through Lorca in the twentieth century.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two things follow for a reader.

An English-trained ear hears assonance as \emph{failure to rhyme} and concludes the poem is unrhymed. It is rhymed — by a rule your ear was not trained on, and the rule is easier than the English one, not harder.

And it explains why Spanish verse can sustain a single rhyme for hundreds of lines where English cannot. Rhyming on vowels alone leaves far more words available. The form is shaped by what the language makes cheap.

That closes the chapter, and with it the last thing this book can teach you about reading: a text carries its date, its register, and its form in details that look like noise until you know what they are.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{asonancia}
  \item whether \emph{luna} and \emph{musa} rhyme in Spanish (yes)
  \item why a Spanish ballad can keep one rhyme for hundreds of lines
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does assonance rhyme on? (The vowels only.) Which form is built on it? (The \emph{romance}, the ballad.) Why can it run so long? (Vowel-only rhyme leaves far more words available.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{What a text tells you before you read it}

\label{lesson:ES-C276-practice}



\begin{quote}
Three details that look like noise until you know what they are — and each one dates or places a text before you have understood a sentence of it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
For each, say what the detail tells you.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item you meet \emph{mas} with no accent — what do you now know about the text? (\textbf{Literary}, and almost certainly not transcribed speech.)
  \item you meet \emph{vuestra merced} — what do you now know? (\textbf{Old}, and you were told long ago what it became: \emph{usted}.)
  \item the lines end \emph{luna … musa … cuna} — is this rhymed? (\textbf{Yes} — assonance, and an English-trained ear will say no.)
\end{itemize}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item which of the three explains something still in use today (\emph{vuestra merced} — it is why \emph{usted} takes the he/she verb)
  \item what all three have in common (each carries information that has nothing to do with what the sentence means)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name what each signals: register, date, form. Which one is a fossil that still governs living grammar? (\emph{Vuestra merced}, behind \emph{usted}.) Which is a rhyme your ear may not hear as one? (Assonance.)
\end{tcolorbox}
